messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence
  Maladaptive Strategies: Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amina is a 74-year-old African American woman who has spent most of her life doing agricultural work, rising before dawn to tend rows of vegetables on a family-run farm outside town. She lives with her partner, a steady man she describes as patient, though in recent years she has kept even him at a careful distance. The rape happened late in the afternoon near the edge of a field after a long workday, when the air smelled of damp soil and cut plants and the farm had gone strangely still. What remains most vivid to her is not a full story she can tell straight through, but the sudden silence in the open land, the smell of earth rising up around her, and the unbearable sense afterward that her body had been violated and spoiled. Each year, as the date approaches, she feels herself tightening days in advance, as if her body already knows what is coming.

In the months after the assault, the farm itself became difficult terrain. When Amina steps outside in the early morning and catches the smell of wet dirt, she is pulled back into the worst parts of what happened, and with that comes an immediate conviction that she is dirty. If the fields fall quiet for even a moment, she feels exposed in a way that is hard to explain to anyone else; the silence does not feel peaceful, only dangerous, and in it she hears again the helplessness of that afternoon. Around the anniversary, these reactions sharpen. She has come to believe not only that what happened ruined her body, but that there is something fundamentally stained about her now, and on those days she can find herself thinking that life may no longer be worth much. The triggers do not remain simple reminders for her; they seem to confirm what she already fears about herself.

Because of this, Amina has gradually narrowed her world. At work she avoids darker storage sheds and any circumstance that feels too enclosed or too much like the place where she was overpowered. If the crew breaks and she notices the smell of turned soil hanging thick in the air, she will busy herself elsewhere or go inside under the pretense of needing water. She no longer tolerates casual touch. A hand on her shoulder from a coworker or even her partner reaching for her in the kitchen can make her recoil. When these moments happen, she tries to clamp down on everything by forcing herself into bright, positive thoughts—telling herself to be grateful, to think of good things, to push the ugliness away. The effort is desperate and rigid rather than soothing, a way of trying not to feel what the smell, the silence, or the date on the calendar has stirred up.

Over time, this way of coping has deepened the very beliefs she is fighting. Avoiding touch has left her more convinced that her body is shameful, as though closeness would expose something contaminated in her. Steering clear of reminders on the farm has not made the fields feel ordinary again; instead, the outdoor smells seem more loaded each season, and her fear of them starts earlier as the anniversary nears. Forcing herself to think only positive thoughts gives her brief moments of control, but when the intrusive sense of dirtiness returns anyway, she takes it as proof that even her own mind cannot be trusted to right itself. Then the thought comes back with more force: maybe life is not worth living if this is what she carries.

These appraisals now shape what she notices everywhere. Because she feels contaminated, she is acutely alert to the smell of soil on her clothes and skin after work, as though the odor itself reveals her defilement. Because she is ashamed of what happened to her body, silence has become hard to bear; in quiet moments she feels trapped with what she believes her body signifies. She responds by tightening her routines further—staying out of certain parts of the farm, keeping her partner from touching her, answering dread with more insistence that she must stay positive—and the more she does this, the more potent those same smells, quiet stretches, and anniversary days become.

What finally brought Amina to treatment was not a single new symptom but the realization that her life had shrunk around these patterns. This past anniversary week, she could not make herself go out to the fields for two days, and when her partner tried gently to comfort her, she jerked away and then wept from shame. She told the clinician she is frightened by how often the thought comes that life may not be worth living, though she also says, quietly, that she wants some part of herself back. More than anything, she hopes to be able to walk onto the land she has worked for decades, smell the earth, and not feel that it is telling her who she is.
